clinicalPearls: The most common autosomal dominant spinocerebellar ataxia worldwide, caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the ATXN3 gene encoding a polyglutamine tract in ataxin-3
Presents with progressive cerebellar ataxia combined with variable pyramidal, extrapyramidal, and peripheral features, giving a broad clinical spectrum
Characteristic signs include prominent, bulging eyes with lid retraction, gaze-evoked nystagmus, and progressive external ophthalmoplegia
Faciolingual fasciculations and myokymia, dystonia, spasticity, and a peripheral neuropathy with amyotrophy are recognised features
Recognised clinical subtypes range from early-onset spastic-dystonic forms to later-onset predominantly ataxic or peripheral-neuropathy phenotypes depending on repeat length and age
Demonstrates anticipation, with earlier onset and greater severity as the repeat expands across generations
Confirmed by molecular testing for the ATXN3 CAG expansion; treatment is symptomatic and multidisciplinary
reference.pathophysiology: Machado-Joseph disease (SCA3) is a polyglutamine disorder caused by expansion of the CAG repeat in the ATXN3 gene. Ataxin-3 normally functions as a deubiquitinating enzyme involved in protein quality control; the expanded polyglutamine tract confers a toxic gain of function, promoting misfolding, aggregation, and formation of neuronal intranuclear inclusions that impair the ubiquitin-proteasome system and cellular homeostasis. Neurodegeneration affects the cerebellum and its connections, brainstem and cranial nerve nuclei, basal ganglia, spinal motor and sensory pathways, and peripheral nerves, accounting for the wide phenotypic range. Repeat length correlates inversely with age at onset, underlying anticipation.
additionalDifferentials: Other dominant spinocerebellar ataxias (SCA1, SCA2, SCA6, SCA7)
Parkinson disease or dystonia syndromes when extrapyramidal features dominate
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis when amyotrophy is prominent
additionalInvestigations: Targeted molecular genetic testing for ATXN3 CAG repeat expansion
Brain MRI showing cerebellar, brainstem, and sometimes basal ganglia atrophy
Nerve conduction studies for associated peripheral neuropathy
Detailed oculomotor examination for ophthalmoplegia and nystagmus
Assessment for dystonia, spasticity, and parkinsonism
Swallowing and speech assessment as bulbar involvement progresses
redFlags: Severe spasticity or dystonia impairing mobility and safety
Respiratory or bulbar decline in advanced disease
reference.prognosis: The disease is progressive over one to several decades with steadily accumulating disability; life expectancy is reduced, usually as a consequence of bulbar dysfunction and respiratory complications, although progression rate varies with subtype.
pitfalls: Attributing the diverse features to separate diagnoses rather than recognising the SCA3 spectrum
Assuming a subtype without gene-specific confirmation
Missing the characteristic bulging eyes and faciolingual fasciculations as diagnostic clues
Neglecting anticipation and genetic counselling for at-risk relatives
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: No disease-modifying therapy exists, so care centres on symptomatic treatment and maintaining function
Physiotherapy, occupational therapy and balance and gait training with walking aids for progressive cerebellar ataxia
Targeted pharmacotherapy for specific features: dopaminergic agents such as levodopa for parkinsonism, baclofen for spasticity, and botulinum toxin for dystonia
Speech and language therapy with swallowing assessment for dysarthria and dysphagia, with attention to aspiration risk
Monitoring and management of complications including falls, contractures, sleep disturbance, depression, and respiratory compromise from bulbar dysfunction
Multidisciplinary neurology-led care with rehabilitation, dietetics and palliative planning as disease advances
Genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant CAG-repeat disorder, with predictive and reproductive testing options and awareness of anticipation
